title: Orthogonal complements and the matrix transpose
lead: This section collects every vector orthogonal to a given subspace into one set, its orthogonal complement, and describes that set as the solutions of a linear system. It then introduces the transpose of a matrix, which writes dot products as a matrix product, and studies its algebraic properties.
summary_html:
This section introduced the matrix transpose, its connection to dot products, and its use in describing the orthogonal complement of a subspace.

  • The columns of the matrix $\kA$ are the rows of the matrix transpose $\kAT$.
  • The components of the product $\kAT\kvecx$ are the dot products of $\kvecx$ with the columns of $\kA$.
  • The orthogonal complement of the column space of $\kA$ equals the null space of $\kAT$; that is, $\kCol(\kA)^\perp = \kNul(\kAT)$.

  • If $\kW$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^p$, then

    $$ \dim \kW + \dim \kWperp = p. $$

exercises.prompt:
1. Sketch the vector $\kvecv=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ on Figure 6.2.1 and one vector that is orthogonal to it.
  2. If a vector $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to $\kvecv$, what do we know about the dot product $\kvecv\cdot\kvecx$?
  3. If we write $\kvecx=\left[\begin{array}{r}x \\ y \end{array}\right]$, use the dot product to write an equation for the vectors orthogonal to $\kvecv$ in terms of $x$ and $y$.
  4. Use this equation to sketch the set of all vectors orthogonal to $\kvecv$ in Figure 6.2.1.
  5. Section 3.5 introduced the column space $\kCol(\kA)$ and null space $\kNul(\kA)$ of a matrix $\kA$. If $\kA$ is a matrix, what is the meaning of the null space $\kNul(\kA)$?
  6. What is the meaning of the column space $\kCol(\kA)$?

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. The vector $\kvecw=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ is an example of a vector orthogonal to $\kvecv$.
  2. The dot product must be zero.
  3. $\kvecv\cdot\kvecx = -x+2y = 0$.
  4. This is the line $y=\frac12 x$.
  5. It is the set of vectors $\kvecx$ for which $\kA\kvecx = \kveczero$.
  6. It is the set of vector $\kvecb$ for which the equation $\kA\kvecx=\kvecb$ is consistent.

exercises.changes: The blank grid of Figure 6.2.1 is left out; the upper panel of Figure 6.2.2 draws the vector v = [−1, 2] and the line of vectors orthogonal to it.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$ form a basis for $\kW$, a two-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^3$. We will find a description of the orthogonal complement $\kWperp$.

  1. Suppose that the vector $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to $\kvecwone$. If we write $\kvecx=\left[\begin{array}{r}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{array}\right]$, use the fact that $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecx = 0$ to write a linear equation for $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$.
  2. Suppose that $\kvecx$ is also orthogonal to $\kvecwtwo$. In the same way, write a linear equation for $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ that arises from the fact that $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecx = 0$.
  3. If $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to both $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$, these two equations give us a linear system $\kB\kvecx=\kveczero$ for some matrix $\kB$. Identify the matrix $\kB$ and write a parametric description of the solution space to the equation $\kB\kvecx = \kveczero$.

  4. Since $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ form a basis for the two-dimensional subspace $\kW$, any vector $\kvecw$ in $\kW$ can be written as a linear combination

    $$ \kvecw = c_1\kvecwone + c_2\kvecwtwo\text{.} $$

    If $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to both $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$, use the distributive property of dot products to explain why $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to $\kvecw$.

  5. Give a basis for the orthogonal complement $\kWperp$ and state the dimension $\dim \kWperp$.
  6. Describe $(\kWperp)^\perp$, the orthogonal complement of $\kWperp$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecx = x_1 - 2x_3 = 0$.
  2. $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecx = x_1+x_2 - x_3 = 0$.
  3. $\kB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ so $\kvecx=x_3\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  4. By distributivity, $(c_1\kvecwone+c_2\kvecwtwo)\cdot\kvecx= c_1\kvecwone\cdot\kvecx + c_2\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecx = 0$.
  5. A basis consists of $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, and $\kWperp$ is one-dimensional.
  6. The orthogonal complement of $\kWperp$ is $\kW$.

Solution.

  1. We have the equation $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecx = x_1 - 2x_3 = 0$.
  2. We have the equation $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecx = x_1+x_2 - x_3 = 0$.

  3. These two equations give $\kB\kvecx=\kveczero$ where

    $$ \kB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{,} $$

    whose solutions have the parametric form $\kvecx=x_3\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

  4. By distributivity, $(c_1\kvecwone+c_2\kvecwtwo)\cdot\kvecx= c_1\kvecwone\cdot\kvecx + c_2\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecx = 0$.
  5. $\kWperp$ is the solution space to the equation $\kB\kvecx=\kveczero$. Therefore, a basis consists of the single vector $\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, and $\kWperp$ is one-dimensional.
  6. Since every vector in $\kWperp$ is orthogonal to every vector in $\kW$, the orthogonal complement of $\kWperp$ is $\kW$.

exercises.prompt:
This activity illustrates how multiplying a vector by $\kAT$ is related to computing dot products with the columns of $\kA$. You’ll develop a better understanding of this relationship if you compute the dot products and matrix products in this activity without using technology.

  1. If $\kB = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \\ \end{bmatrix}$, write the matrix $\kBT$.

  2. Suppose that

    $$ \kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecw=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$

    Find the dot products $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecw$ and $\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecw$.

  3. Now write the matrix $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} \kvecvone & \kvecvtwo \end{bmatrix}$ and its transpose $\kAT$. Find the product $\kAT\kvecw$ and describe how this product computes both dot products $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecw$ and $\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecw$.
  4. Suppose that $\kvecx$ is a vector that is orthogonal to both $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$. What does this say about the dot products $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecx$ and $\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecx$? What does this say about the product $\kAT\kvecx$?
  5. Use the matrix $\kAT$ to give a parametric description of all the vectors $\kvecx$ that are orthogonal to $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.
  6. Remember that $\kNul(\kAT)$, the null space of $\kAT$, is the solution set of the equation $\kAT\kvecx=\kveczero$. If $\kvecx$ is a vector in $\kNul(\kAT)$, explain why $\kvecx$ must be orthogonal to both $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.
  7. Remember that $\kCol(\kA)$, the column space of $\kA$, is the set of linear combinations of the columns of $\kA$. Therefore, any vector in $\kCol(\kA)$ can be written as $c_1\kvecvone+c_2\kvecvtwo$. If $\kvecx$ is a vector in $\kNul(\kAT)$, explain why $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to every vector in $\kCol(\kA)$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kAT = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecw =-10$, $\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecw =6$.
  3. $$ \kAT\kvecw =\left[\begin{array}{r}\kvecvone\cdot\kvecw \\ \kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecw \end{array}\right] $$
  4. $\kAT\kvecx = \kveczero$.
  5. $\kvecx=x_3\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  6. $\kAT\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}\kvecvone\cdot\kvecx \\ \kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecx \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.
  7. Apply the distributive property of dot products.

Solution.

  1. $\kAT = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecvone\cdot\kvecw &{}={} 2(-2) + 0(2) + (-2)3 &{}={} -10 \\ \kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecw &{}={} 1(-2) + 1(2) + 2(3) &{}={} 6 \end{aligned} $$
  3. $$ \kAT\kvecw = \left[\begin{array}{r}2(-2)+0(2)+(-2)3 \\ 1(-2)+1(2)+2(3) \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}-10 \\ 6 \end{array}\right] =\left[\begin{array}{r}\kvecvone\cdot\kvecw \\ \kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecw \end{array}\right] $$
  4. Both dot products are 0 so we have $\kAT\kvecx = \kveczero$.

  5. We need to solve the equation $\kAT\kvecx = \kveczero$ so we find the reduced row echelon form

    $$ \kAT \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

    The vectors orthogonal to both $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$ have the form $\kvecx=x_3\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

  6. $\kAT\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}\kvecvone\cdot\kvecx \\ \kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecx \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ tells us that $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecx=0$ and $\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecx=0$.

  7. Since $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to both $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$, we have

    $$ (c_1\kvecvone+c_2\kvecvtwo)\cdot\kvecx = c_1\kvecvone\cdot\kvecx + c_2\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecx = 0 $$

exercises.prompt:
In Sage, the transpose of a matrix A is given by A.T. Define the matrices

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{6pt} \kB = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{6pt} \kC= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$
  1. Evaluate $(\kA+\kB)^T$ and $\kAT+\kBT$. What do you notice about the relationship between these two matrices?
  2. What happens if you transpose a matrix twice; that is, what is $(\kAT)^T$?
  3. Find $\det(\kC)$ and $\det(\kCT)$. What do you notice about the relationship between these determinants?
    1. Find the product $\kA\kC$ and its transpose $(\kA\kC)^T$.
    2. Is it possible to compute the product $\kAT\kCT$? Explain why or why not.
    3. Find the product $\kCT\kAT$ and compare it to $(\kA\kC)^T$. What do you notice about the relationship between these two matrices?
  5. What is the transpose of the identity matrix $\kI$?
  6. If a square matrix $\kD$ is invertible, explain why you can guarantee that $\kD^T$ is invertible and why $(\kD^T)^{-1} = (\kD^{-1})^T$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $(\kA+\kB)^T = \kAT + \kBT$.
  2. $(\kAT)^T = \kA$.
  3. $\det(\kCT) = \det(\kC)$
  4. $(\kA\kC)^T=\kCT\kAT$.
  5. $\kI^T=\kI$
  6. $(\kD^T)^{-1} = (\kD^{-1})^T$.

Solution.

  1. $(\kA+\kB)^T = \kAT + \kBT$.
  2. $(\kAT)^T = \kA$.
  3. $\det(\kCT) = \det(\kC)$
    1. $\kA\kC = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & -6 & -3 \\ 1 & 6 & -8 \end{bmatrix}$ and $(\kA\kC)^T = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 1 \\ -6 & 6 \\ -3 & -8 \end{bmatrix}$
    2. The product $\kAT\kCT$ is not defined because $\kAT$ has two columns and $\kCT$ has three rows.
    3. $(\kA\kC)^T=\kCT\kAT$
  5. $\kI^T=\kI$
  6. We have $\kD\kD^{-1} = \kI$ so $(\kD\kD^{-1})^T = (\kD^{-1})^T\kD^T = \kI^T=\kI$. This means that $(\kD^T)^{-1} = (\kD^{-1})^T$.

exercises.prompt:
1. Suppose that $\kW$ is a $5$-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^9$ and that $\kA$ is a matrix whose columns form a basis for $\kW$; that is, $\kCol(\kA) = \kW$.

    1. What is the shape of $\kA$?
    2. What is the rank of $\kA$?
    3. What is the shape of $\kAT$?
    4. What is the rank of $\kAT$?
    5. What is $\dim\kNul(\kAT)$?
    6. What is $\dim \kWperp$?
    7. How are the dimensions of $\kW$ and $\kWperp$ related?

  2. Suppose that $\kW$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^4$ having basis

    $$ \kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 2 \\ -6 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]. $$
    1. Find the dimensions $\dim \kW$ and $\dim \kWperp$.
    2. Find a basis for $\kWperp$. It may be helpful to know that the Sage command A.right_kernel() produces a basis for $\kNul(\kA)$.
    3. Verify that each of the basis vectors you found for $\kWperp$ are orthogonal to the basis vectors for $\kW$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

    1. $9\times 5$
    2. $5$
    3. $5\times 9$
    4. $5$
    5. $4$
    6. $4$
    7. $\dim \kW + \dim \kWperp = 9$
    1. $2$
    2. $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ .
    3. Verify by computing the four dot products.

Solution.

    1. $\kA$ is $9\times 5$.
    2. $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 5$.
    3. $\kAT$ is $5\times 9$.
    4. $\operatorname{rank}(\kAT) = 5$
    5. $\dim \kNul(\kAT) = 9 - 5 = 4$
    6. $\dim \kWperp = \dim\kNul(\kAT) = 4$
    7. $\dim \kW + \dim \kWperp = 9$ since the subspaces live in ${\mathbb R}^9$.
    1. $\dim \kW = 2$ so $\dim \kWperp = 4-2=2$.
    2. A basis is $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ .
    3. You can verify by computing the four dot products.

exercises.prompt: Vectors in $\kW$ and $\kWperp$. Can a nonzero vector be in both $\kW$ and $\kWperp$? Explain your thinking.

answer.solution: No. Suppose a vector $\kvecv$ is in both $\kW$ and $\kWperp$. Because $\kvecv$ is in $\kWperp$, it is orthogonal to every vector in $\kW$, and $\kvecv$ is itself one of the vectors in $\kW$, so $\kvecv$ is orthogonal to itself: $\kvecv\cdot\kvecv = 0$. But $\kvecv\cdot\kvecv = |\kvecv|^2$, the square of its length, so $|\kvecv| = 0$ and $\kvecv = \kveczero$. The only vector in both $\kW$ and $\kWperp$ is the zero vector.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kW$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^4$ with basis

$$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -4 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \\ -5 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. What are the dimensions $\dim \kW$ and $\dim \kWperp$?
  2. Find a basis for $\kWperp$.
  3. Verify that each of the basis vectors for $\kWperp$ are orthogonal to $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\dim \kW = 2$ and $\dim \kWperp = 2$.
  2. $\kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$
  3. Use the dot product.

Solution.

  1. $\dim \kW = 2$ and $\dim \kWperp = 4-2 = 2$.
  2. $\kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$
  3. Verify that $\mathbf{w}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_j = 0$ for all $i$ and $j$.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the matrix $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

  1. Find $\operatorname{rank}(\kA)$ and a basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.
  2. Determine the dimension of $\kCol(\kA)^\perp$ and find a basis for it.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 2$ and a basis for $\kCol(\kA)$ is $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ and $\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$
  2. $\dim\kCol(\kA)^\perp = 1$ with basis $\left[\begin{array}{r}5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

Solution.

  1. $\kA\sim\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ so $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 2$ since there are two pivot positions. The reduced row echelon form shows that the third column is a linear combination of the first two so $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ and $\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ form a basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.
  2. We know that $\dim \kCol(\kA)^\perp = 3 - 2 = 1$. To find a basis, solve the equation $\kAT\kvecx = \kveczero$ to obtain $\left[\begin{array}{r}5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kW$ is the subspace of ${\mathbb R}^4$ defined as the solution set of the equation

$$ x_1 - 3x_2 + 5x_3 - 2x_4 = 0. $$
  1. What are the dimensions $\dim \kW$ and $\dim \kWperp$?
  2. Find a basis for $\kW$.
  3. Find a basis for $\kWperp$.

  4. In general, how can you easily find a basis for $\kWperp$ when $\kW$ is defined by

    $$ Ax_1+Bx_2+Cx_3+Dx_4 = 0? $$

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\dim \kW = 3$, $\dim \kWperp = 1$.
  2. $\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, $\left[\begin{array}{r}-5 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, and $\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ 5 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$
  4. $\left[\begin{array}{r}A \\ B \\ C \\ D \end{array}\right]$

Solution.

  1. $\kW = \kNul(\kB)$ where $\kB = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ so $\dim \kW = 4 -1 =3$. Therefore, $\dim \kWperp = 4-3 = 1$.
  2. A basis for $\kW$ is $\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, $\left[\begin{array}{r}-5 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, and $\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. Since every vector in $\kW$ satisfies $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ 5 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]\cdot\kvecx = 0$, a basis for $\kWperp$ is $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ 5 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$
  4. $\left[\begin{array}{r}A \\ B \\ C \\ D \end{array}\right]$

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether the following statements are true or false and explain your reasoning.

  1. If $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then $\kvecx=\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ -5 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ is in $\kCol(\kA)^\perp$.
  2. If $\kA$ is a $2\times3$ matrix and $\kB$ is a $3\times4$ matrix, then $(\kA\kB)^T = \kAT\kBT$ is a $4\times2$ matrix.
  3. If the columns of $\kA$ are $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$ and $\kAT\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, then $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to $\kvecvtwo$.
  4. If $\kA$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 3$, then $\kCol(\kA)^\perp$ is a line in ${\mathbb R}^4$.
  5. If $\kA$ is a $5\times 7$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 5$, then $\operatorname{rank}(\kAT) = 7$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. True
  2. False
  3. True
  4. True
  5. False

Solution.

  1. True, since $\kAT\kvecx=\kveczero$, $\kvecx$ is in $\kCol(\kA)^\perp$.
  2. False, $(\kA\kB)^T$ is a $4\times2$ matrix, but it is given by $(\kA\kB)^T=\kBT\kAT$.
  3. True, because the second component of $\kAT\kvecx = \kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecx=0$.
  4. True, because $\dim\kCol(\kA)^\perp = 4-\dim\kCol(\kA) = 4-3 = 1$.
  5. False, $\operatorname{rank}(\kAT) = \operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 5$.

exercises.prompt:
Apply properties of matrix operations to simplify the following expressions.

  1. $\kAT(\kB\kAT)^{-1}$
  2. $(\kA+\kB)^T(\kA+\kB)$
  3. $[\kA(\kA+\kB)^T]^T$
  4. $(\kA + 2\kI)^T$

A symmetric matrix $\kA$ is one for which $\kA=\kAT$.

  1. Explain why a symmetric matrix must be square.
  2. If $\kA$ and $\kB$ are general matrices and $\kD$ is a square diagonal matrix, which of the following matrices can you guarantee are symmetric?
    1. $\kD$
    2. $\kB\kA\kB^{-1}$
    3. $\kA\kAT$.
    4. $\kB\kD\kBT$

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. They must have the same number of rows and columns.
    1. Yes
    2. No
    3. No
    4. Yes

Solution.

  1. If $\kA$ is an $m\times n$ matrix, then $\kAT$ is $n\times m$ If these matrices are the same, then $m=n$.
    1. If $\kD$ is diagonal, then $\kD^T = \kD$.
    2. $(\kB\kA\kB^{-1})^T = (\kB^{-1})^T\kAT\kBT$ so this matrix need not be symmetric.
    3. $(\kA\kAT)^T = (\kAT)^T\kAT = \kA\kAT$ so this matrix is symmetric.
    4. $(\kB\kD\kBT)^T = (\kBT)^T\kD^T\kBT = \kB\kD\kBT$ so this matrix is symmetric.

exercises.prompt:
If $\kA$ is a square matrix, remember that the characteristic polynomial of $\kA$ is $\det(\kA-\klambda \kI)$ and that the roots of the characteristic polynomial are the eigenvalues of $\kA$.

  1. Explain why $\kA$ and $\kAT$ have the same characteristic polynomial.
  2. Explain why $\kA$ and $\kAT$ have the same set of eigenvalues.
  3. Suppose that $\kA$ is diagonalizable with diagonalization $\kA=\kP\kD\kPinv$. Explain why $\kAT$ is diagonalizable and find a diagonalization.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Use properties of the matrix transpose.
  2. Because they have the same characteristic polynomial.
  3. $\kAT = (\kP^T)^{-1} \kD \kP^T$

Solution.

  1. $(\kA-\klambda \kI)^T = \kAT - \klambda \kI$ and therefore $\det(\kAT-\klambda \kI) = \det[(\kA-\klambda \kI)^T] = \det(\kA-\klambda \kI)$.
  2. The eigenvalues of a matrix are given by the roots of its characteristic polynomial. Since $\kA$ and $\kAT$ have the same characteristic polynomial, they have the same eigenvalues.
  3. $\kAT = (\kP\kD\kPinv)^T = (\kP^T)^{-1} \kD \kP^T$

exercises.prompt:
This exercise introduces a version of the Pythagorean theorem that we’ll use later.

  1. Suppose that $\kvecv$ and $\kvecw$ are orthogonal to one another. Use the dot product to explain why

    $$ \left|\kvecv+\kvecw\right|^2 = \left|\kvecv\right|^2 + \left|\kvecw\right|^2. $$

  2. Suppose that $\kW$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^m$ and that $\kvecz$ is a vector in ${\mathbb R}^m$ for which

    $$ \kvecz = \kvecx + \kvecy, $$

    where $\kvecx$ is in $\kW$ and $\kvecy$ is in $\kWperp$. Explain why

    $$ \left|\kvecz\right|^2 = \left|\kvecx\right|^2 + \left|\kvecy\right|^2, $$

    which is an expression of the Pythagorean theorem.

In the next chapter, symmetric matrices—that is, matrices for which $\kA=\kAT$—play an important role. It turns out that eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix that are associated to different eigenvalues are orthogonal. We will explain this fact in this exercise.

  1. Viewing a vector as a matrix having one column, we may write $\kvecx\cdot\kvecy = \kvecx^T\kvecy$. If $\kA$ is a matrix, explain why $\kvecx\cdot (\kA\kvecy) = (\kAT\kvecx) \cdot \kvecy$.
  2. We have seen that the matrix $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvectors $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, with associated eigenvalue $\klambdaone=3$, and $\kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$, with associated eigenvalue $\klambdatwo = -1$. Verify that $\kA$ is symmetric and that $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$ are orthogonal.
  3. Suppose that $\kA$ is a general symmetric matrix and that $\kvecvone$ is an eigenvector associated to eigenvalue $\klambdaone$ and that $\kvecvtwo$ is an eigenvector associated to a different eigenvalue $\klambdatwo$. Beginning with $\kvecvone\cdot (\kA\kvecvtwo)$, apply the identity from the first part of this exercise to explain why $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$ are orthogonal.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Use properties of the transpose.
  2. Compute the dot product of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.
  3. It follows that $(\klambdaone-\klambdatwo)\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo = 0$

Solution.

  1. $\kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecy) = \kvecx^T\kA\kvecy = (\kAT\kvecx)^T\kvecy = (\kAT\kvecx)\cdot\kvecy$.
  2. $\kAT = \kA$ and $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo=0$.
  3. $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecvone\cdot(\kA\kvecvtwo) & {}={} (\kA\kvecvone)\cdot\kvecvtwo \\ \klambdatwo\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo & {}={} \klambdaone\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo \\ (\klambdaone-\klambdatwo)\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo&{}={} 0 \end{aligned} $$

    so $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo=0$ since $\klambdaone-\klambdatwo\neq 0$.

exercises.prompt:
Given an $m\times n$ matrix $\kA$, the row space of $\kA$ is the column space of $\kAT$; that is, $\text{Row}(\kA) = \kCol(\kAT)$.

  1. Suppose that $\kA$ is a $7\times 15$ matrix. For what $p$ is $\text{Row}(\kA)$ a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^p$?
  2. How can Proposition 6.2.10 help us describe $\text{Row}(\kA)^\perp$?
  3. Suppose that $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Find bases for $\text{Row}(\kA)$ and $\text{Row}(\kA)^\perp$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $p=15$
  2. $\text{Row}(\kA)^\perp = \ \kNul(\kA)$
  3. A basis for $\text{Row}(\kA)$ are the three rows of $\kA$. A basis for $\text{Row}(\kA)^\perp = \kNul(\kA)$ is $\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.

Solution.

  1. Since $\kAT$ is $15\times7$, it follows that $\text{Row}(\kA)=\kCol(\kAT)$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^{15}$.
  2. $\text{Row}(\kA)^\perp = \kCol(\kAT)^\perp = \kNul((\kAT)^T) = \kNul(\kA)$
  3. $\operatorname{rank}(\kA) = 3$ so $\operatorname{rank}(\kAT)=\dim\kCol(\kAT) = \dim\text{Row}(\kA) = 3$. A basis for $\text{Row}(\kA)$ are the three rows of $\kA$. $\text{Row}(\kA)^\perp = \kNul(\kA)$ is one-dimensional with basis $\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.

footnotes.html: The book’s answer prints the basis vector $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, which is not orthogonal to $\kvecwone$: $\kvecwone\cdot\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] = 1 - 2 = -1$. The basis vector of $\kWperp$ is $\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, as part c’s parametric description and the solution give.
The book writes $\kAT$ here and in the solution where the part asks for $\kBT$; the matrix shown, $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, is $\kBT$.
The book’s answer says No for $\kA\kAT$, but its solution shows $(\kA\kAT)^T = (\kAT)^T\kAT = \kA\kAT$, so $\kA\kAT$ is always symmetric: the answer is Yes.

The null space of a matrix with $m$ columns has dimension $m$ minus its rank, and $\kAT$, an $n\times m$ matrix, has $m$ columns.
The columns $\kvecwone, \kvecwtwo, \ldots, \kvecwn$ of $\kA$ form a basis of $\kW$, so $\kCol(\kA) = \kW$.
